description: int() on a negative float rounds down (toward negative infinity) rather than truncating toward zero, so int(-3.9) is believed to be -4.
Believing float('nan') == float('nan') is True; NaN is never equal to anything, including itself.
Believing / performs integer division when both operands are ints, so 7 / 2 gives 3 instead of the float 3.5.
Believing the % operator takes the sign of the dividend as in C, so -7 % 3 is -1 rather than 2 (Python's result takes the divisor's sign).
Believing -2 ** 2 equals 4 because unary minus is applied before **; actually ** binds tighter, giving -4.
Believing 1 < 2 < 3 is evaluated as (1 < 2) < 3 rather than as (1 < 2) and (2 < 3).
Believing and/or always return True or False, rather than returning one of their operands, so 3 or 5 is thought to be True.
Believing bool is unrelated to int, so True == 1 is False or errors; in fact bool subclasses int.
Believing == None and is None are always equivalent, ignoring that a custom __eq__ can change the result of == None.
Believing isinstance takes several types as separate arguments or a list, rather than a single tuple of types.
Believing tuples and strings support item assignment like lists, so t[0] = 5 or s[0] = 'H' succeeds.
Believing a slice with an out-of-range bound raises IndexError, when slices silently clamp to the sequence's ends.
Believing the stop index of a slice is inclusive, so [1:3] includes the element at index 3.
Believing [[]] * 3 creates three independent inner lists, when it repeats references to the same list.
Believing a = b = c = [] gives three separate lists rather than three names bound to one list.
Believing list2 = list1 copies the list, so mutating list2 won't affect list1.
Believing lst[:] returns a reference to the same list rather than a new shallow copy.
Believing append and extend behave identically, or that append with a list spreads its elements into the target list.
Believing list.sort() returns the sorted list, when it sorts in place and returns None.
Believing lst.pop() with no argument removes the first element rather than the last.
Confusing list.remove(value), which removes by value, with pop(index), which removes by position and returns the item.
Believing zip pads shorter inputs with None, when it stops at the shortest iterable.
Believing reversed() returns a list that can be indexed, when it returns an iterator.
Believing map() and filter() return lists directly rather than lazy iterators needing list() to materialize.
Believing len() does not work on sets, when it works on all built-in sized containers.
Believing range(n) includes n, so list(range(5)) has 6 elements ending in 5.
Believing a list can be a dict key if its contents don't change; lists are unhashable regardless.
Believing 'x' in d checks a dict's values rather than its keys.
Believing membership tests on a list are O(1) like on sets and dicts, rather than O(n).
Believing dict iteration order is arbitrary in modern Python, when it follows insertion order since 3.7.
Believing split() and split(' ') behave the same, missing that split(' ') yields empty strings for adjacent spaces.
Believing string methods like replace, strip, or lower modify the string in place rather than returning a new one.
Believing int('42.5') returns 42 by truncating, when it raises ValueError.
Believing the string '0' or 'False' is falsy because of its content; any non-empty string is truthy.
Believing round() always rounds halves up as taught in school, when Python rounds half to even, so round(2.5) is 2.
Believing (1) is a one-element tuple, when the trailing comma in (1,) is what makes it a tuple.
Believing a function can assign to a module-level variable without the global keyword, or that assignment later in a function leaves earlier reads using the global.
Believing a loop's else clause runs when the loop exits via break, rather than only when it completes without break.
Believing that after an exception is caught, execution resumes inside the try block or the exception is automatically re-raised.
Believing multiple exceptions are caught with 'except A or B' or 'except A, B' rather than a tuple.
